claims.claim: The Lifers Group at Rahway created the Juvenile Awareness Program in 1976.

claims.claim: The Petrosino (Campbell Collaboration) systematic review meta-analyzed nine randomized trials of juvenile awareness programs, with literature coverage spanning 1967-1992.
claims.episode_span: A 2002 Campbell Collaboration systematic review examined nine randomized and quasi-randomized evaluations conducted between 1967 and 1992

claims.claim: A meta-analysis of Scared Straight and similar programs found they actively increased crime and re-offense rates compared with controls
claims.episode_span: the pooled odds ratio was 1.68 — youths who went through the programs were roughly 68 percent more likely to offend than those who did not
claims.supporting_quote: A meta-analysis of the results of a number of Scared Straight and similar programs found that they actively increased crime rates and lead to higher re-offense rates compared to control groups

claims.claim: James Finckenauer, a Rutgers School of Criminal Justice professor, ran a controlled test of the Scared Straight program starting in 1978 and concluded attendees were more likely to commit crimes than non-attendees.
claims.episode_span: A few criminologists at the time, including some at Rutgers University, questioned whether the emotional intensity might produce reactance rather than deterrence, but those cautions received little attention amid the rapid expansion.
claims.supporting_quote: In April 1978, James Finckenauer, a professor of the Rutgers School of Criminal Justice, began a test of the Scared Straight program, using a control group , something that had not been done previously.
